newsitem.title: USA: Cult's comet connection has historic precedent.
newsitem.headline: Cult's comet connection has historic precedent.

text.p: Mention of Comet Hale-Bopp by Internet-savvy members of a suicide cult is in keeping with superstitions that have attended comets for thousands of years, an astronomy historian said on Thursday.

"Initially comets were thought to be an atmospheric phenomenon ... then in the Middle Ages comets were thought to be warning shots fired at a sinful Earth from the right hand of a vengeful god," Donald Yeomans of the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, California, said by telephone.

Hale-Bopp, an especially bright, easy-to-see comet that made its closest pass to Earth this week, has been the focus of intense scientific scrutiny, but a spokesman for the Space Telescope Science Institute called it "a plain old comet."
Nevertheless, Hale-Bopp was mentioned on an Internet site linked to 39 people found dead in a mass suicide in a mansion in Rancho Santa Fe, California, near San Diego.
This Internet site, entitled "Heaven's Gate," referred to the possibility that Hale-Bopp might be shielding a space ship that would take believers to heaven.

"Whether Hale-Bopp has a 'companion' or not is irrelevant from our perspective," the site's message said. "However, its arrival is joyously very significant to us at 'Heaven's Gate'. The joy is that our Older Member in the Evolutionary Level Above Human (The 'King of Heaven') has made it clear to us that Hale-Bopp's approach is the 'marker' we've been waiting for -- the time for the arrival of the spacecraft from the Level Above Human to take us home to 'Their World' -- in the literal Heavens."
Yeomans, author of the book "Comets: a Chronological History of Observation, Science, Myth and Folklore," said such links between comets and death have historic precedent.

One early reference to a fateful comet appearance occurred in 44 B.C., when the Roman Emperor Augustus dedicated a temple to a comet visible during athletic games in that year, just after the assassination of Julius Caesar.

"The common people assumed that it was the soul of Caesar on its way to the region of the immortal gods," Yeomans wrote. Augustus used a comet on some coins struck during his rule, "perhaps to remind his subjects that the reins of power had passed to him from the hands of his now deified father."
The coming of comets has frequently prompted apocalyptic fears, Yeomans said.

As scientists learned more about comets -- notably that some comets' orbits intercept Earth's orbit -- "there was gradual transformation of comets as warnings to agents of destruction," according to Yeomans.

In 1773, Paris was sent into a panic after Joseph-Jerome Lefrancais de Lalande summarized a paper on his computations that 61 comets had orbits that brought them close to Earth. He knew that any chance of a collision was slight, but apparently failed to emphasise this point.

The great comet of 1843 saw another end-of-the-world scenario, advanced by William Miller and his followers, the Millerites. The comet was seen as a celestial sign confirming Miller's belief that the Earth would be destroyed by fire. But the Earth did not end as predicted on April 3 of that year.
Another comet scare occurred in Paris in 1857, Yeomans wrote, but it was "all the more unfounded because no real comet was involved."
As regards Hale-Bopp, scientists are revelling in its large size, active nucleus and relatively close proximity to Earth.
Ray Villard, a spokesman for the Space Telescope Science Institute, which analyses images from the orbiting Hubble Space Telescope, said of Hale-Bopp, "It's a plain old comet."

Lucy McFadden, an astronomer at the University of Maryland, was troubled by the cult's reference to Hale-Bopp: "It's ironic in the day of the World Wide Web, when there's so much information available, that there are people who choose to have their beliefs take them so far from the truth."
